title: Electric Current and its Effects
description: Grade 7 Physics: Electric Current and its Effects — concept notes, solved examples, key-point recaps, per-topic quizzes and free online tests.

topics.title: Electric Circuits and Their Symbols
topics.concept:
Electricity powers almost everything around us, from lights and fans to phones and computers. The flow of electric charge through a conducting path is called an electric current. For a current to flow, there must be a complete, unbroken path for it to travel along. This complete path is called an electric circuit. A basic circuit needs three essential parts: a source of electricity (such as a cell or battery), connecting wires to carry the current, and a device that uses the current (such as a bulb). A switch is usually added to turn the current on and off.

A circuit works only when it is closed (complete) — that is, when there is an unbroken conducting path from one terminal of the cell, through the wires and devices, and back to the other terminal. When the path is broken at any point, for example by an open switch, it becomes an open circuit, and no current flows, so the bulb does not glow. Turning a switch ON closes the circuit; turning it OFF opens it.

Drawing every component as a realistic picture would be slow and confusing, so scientists use simple, standard circuit symbols to represent each part. A cell is shown as one long thin line (the positive terminal) and one short thick line (the negative terminal); a battery is two or more cells joined together. A switch is shown as a small gap with a lever that can be open or closed; a bulb is shown as a circle with a cross or a loop inside; connecting wires are drawn as straight lines; and an ammeter (which measures current) is shown as a circle with the letter A inside. A diagram drawn using these symbols is called a circuit diagram, and it lets anyone understand and build the circuit easily.

The current in a circuit is taken to flow from the positive terminal of the cell, through the external circuit, to the negative terminal — this is called the conventional direction of current.

examples.problem: Example 1: A bulb in a circuit does not glow even though the cell is new. The switch is found to be open. Explain why the bulb is off.
examples.solution:
A bulb glows only when current flows through it.

  • An open switch creates a gap in the conducting path, making the circuit open.
  • With a broken path, no current can flow from the cell to the bulb.
  • Answer: The open switch breaks the circuit, so no current flows and the bulb does not glow.
examples.answer: The open switch breaks the circuit, so no current flows and the bulb does not glow.

examples.problem: Example 2: Why do scientists use symbols instead of drawing realistic pictures in a circuit diagram?
examples.solution:
Realistic drawings are slow and unclear.

  • Standard symbols are simple, quick to draw, and understood everywhere.
  • They make a circuit diagram easy to read and to build from.
  • Answer: Symbols are used because they are simple, standard, and make circuit diagrams quick to draw and easy to understand.
examples.answer: Symbols are used because they are simple, standard, and make circuit diagrams quick to draw and easy to understand.

examples.problem: Example 3: In a cell symbol, which line represents the positive terminal?
examples.solution:
A cell symbol has two lines of different size.

  • The longer, thinner line stands for the positive terminal.
  • The shorter, thicker line stands for the negative terminal.
  • Answer: The longer, thinner line represents the positive terminal of the cell.
examples.answer: The longer, thinner line represents the positive terminal of the cell.

recap:
• An electric current is the flow of electric charge through a conducting path.
  • A complete circuit needs a source (cell/battery), connecting wires, and a device, usually with a switch.
  • Current flows only in a closed (complete) circuit; an open circuit (broken path) carries no current.
  • Standard circuit symbols represent the cell, battery, switch, bulb, wire, and ammeter in a circuit diagram.
  • Conventional current flows from the positive terminal of the cell through the circuit to the negative terminal.

topics.title: Series and Parallel Circuits
topics.concept:
When a circuit contains more than one device, such as two or more bulbs, the devices can be connected in two different ways: in series or in parallel. The way they are connected changes how the circuit behaves.

In a series circuit, the components are connected one after another in a single loop, so the same current flows through each component in turn. There is only one path for the current. The main feature — and limitation — of a series circuit is that if any one component fails or its connection breaks, the whole circuit becomes open and all the devices stop working. This is exactly what happens in some older sets of decorative lights: when one bulb fuses, the entire string goes dark. Also, when more bulbs are added in series, each bulb glows more dimly, because they share the same current along one path.

In a parallel circuit, the components are connected on separate branches, so the current has more than one path to flow through. Each device gets its own connection across the source. The key advantage is that each device works independently: if one bulb fuses or is switched off, the others keep working because they still have a complete path of their own. Bulbs connected in parallel also glow at their full, normal brightness, because each receives the full supply.

This is why the wiring in homes is done in parallel: every light, fan, and socket is on its own branch, so each can be switched on or off separately without affecting the others, and each runs at full brightness. A series connection, by contrast, is useful where we want all components to be controlled together or where the same current must pass through each — such as in a simple torch where the bulb and switch lie in one loop. Understanding the difference helps us choose the right connection for each purpose.

examples.problem: Example 1: In a string of decorative lights connected in series, one bulb fuses and the whole string goes dark. Explain why.
examples.solution:
A series circuit has only one path for the current.

  • All the bulbs lie one after another in a single loop.
  • When one bulb fuses, it breaks this single path, making the whole circuit open.
  • Answer: The fused bulb breaks the only current path, so the circuit is open and all the bulbs go dark.
examples.answer: The fused bulb breaks the only current path, so the circuit is open and all the bulbs go dark.

examples.problem: Example 2: Why is the electrical wiring in houses done in parallel rather than in series?
examples.solution:
Home appliances must work independently and at full power.

  • In a parallel circuit each device is on its own branch with its own path.
  • So each light or fan can be switched on or off separately and runs at full brightness, and one failing does not affect the others.
  • Answer: Parallel wiring lets each appliance work independently at full brightness, which is why homes are wired in parallel.
examples.answer: Parallel wiring lets each appliance work independently at full brightness, which is why homes are wired in parallel.

examples.problem: Example 3: Two identical bulbs are connected first in series and then in parallel to the same cell. In which case do they glow brighter?
examples.solution:
Brightness depends on how much current each bulb receives.

  • In series, the two bulbs share a single path, so each glows dimmer.
  • In parallel, each bulb gets its own full connection to the cell, so each glows at full brightness.
  • Answer: The bulbs glow brighter when connected in parallel, because each receives the full supply.
examples.answer: The bulbs glow brighter when connected in parallel, because each receives the full supply.

recap:
• In a series circuit, components are joined one after another in a single loop, and the same current flows through each.
  • If one component in a series circuit fails, the whole circuit breaks and all devices stop working.
  • In a parallel circuit, components are on separate branches, giving the current more than one path.
  • In a parallel circuit, each device works independently and at full brightness; failure of one does not affect the others.
  • House wiring is done in parallel so each appliance can be controlled separately and runs at full power.

topics.title: Heating Effect of Electric Current
topics.concept:
When an electric current flows through a wire, the wire becomes warm. This warming of a conductor by an electric current is called the heating effect of electric current. The heat is produced because the moving charges have to push their way through the material of the wire, and the material opposes their flow. This opposition to the flow of current is called resistance. The greater the resistance of a wire, the more heat is produced when current flows through it for a given current.

The amount of heat produced depends on three things: the amount of current flowing (more current produces more heat), the resistance of the wire (higher resistance produces more heat), and the time for which the current flows (longer time produces more heat). Thin wires and special alloy wires have high resistance and so heat up strongly, while thick copper wires have low resistance and stay cool.

The heating effect has many useful applications. Many everyday appliances work by deliberately using a high-resistance wire that gets very hot when current passes through it. Examples include the electric heater, electric iron, toaster, electric kettle, geyser (water heater), and hair dryer. The electric bulb also uses this effect: a thin tungsten filament with high resistance gets white-hot and glows, giving off light. These heating elements are usually made of an alloy called nichrome, because nichrome has high resistance, does not melt easily even when red-hot, and does not get spoilt (oxidise) quickly in air.

A very important safety use of the heating effect is the electric fuse. A fuse is a short piece of thin wire made of a metal with a low melting point, connected in the circuit. If too much current flows — for example during a short circuit or overloading — the fuse wire heats up, melts, and breaks the circuit, stopping the current. This protects appliances and wiring from being damaged or catching fire. Modern homes also use devices called MCBs (miniature circuit breakers) that switch off automatically for the same reason.

examples.problem: Example 1: Why does the coil of an electric heater become red-hot while the connecting copper wires stay cool?
examples.solution:
Heat produced depends on resistance.

  • The heater coil is made of a high-resistance alloy, so it strongly opposes the current and produces a lot of heat, becoming red-hot.
  • The copper connecting wires have very low resistance, so they produce very little heat and stay cool.
  • Answer: The high-resistance coil heats up greatly while the low-resistance copper wires stay cool.
examples.answer: The high-resistance coil heats up greatly while the low-resistance copper wires stay cool.

examples.problem: Example 2: How does an electric fuse protect household wiring and appliances?
examples.solution:
A fuse uses the heating effect for safety.

  • A fuse is a thin wire of low melting point connected in the circuit.
  • If the current becomes too large, the fuse heats up, melts, and breaks the circuit, stopping the current.
  • Answer: The fuse melts and breaks the circuit when excess current flows, protecting the wiring and appliances.
examples.answer: The fuse melts and breaks the circuit when excess current flows, protecting the wiring and appliances.

examples.problem: Example 3: Why are the heating elements of appliances made of nichrome rather than copper?
examples.solution:
A heating element must get hot and survive high temperatures.

  • Nichrome has high resistance, so it produces a lot of heat, and it does not melt or get spoilt easily even when red-hot.
  • Copper has very low resistance and would not produce enough heat.
  • Answer: Nichrome is used because it has high resistance, withstands high temperatures, and does not spoil easily, unlike copper.
examples.answer: Nichrome is used because it has high resistance, withstands high temperatures, and does not spoil easily, unlike copper.

recap:
• The heating effect of electric current is the production of heat when current flows through a conductor.
  • Resistance is the opposition offered by a material to the flow of current; higher resistance produces more heat.
  • Heat produced depends on the current, the resistance, and the time for which the current flows.
  • Appliances such as heaters, irons, toasters, kettles, and bulbs work using the heating effect; elements are made of nichrome.
  • An electric fuse is a thin low-melting-point wire that melts and breaks the circuit during excess current, protecting it.

topics.title: Magnetic Effect of Current and the Electromagnet
topics.concept:
Electric current does more than produce heat — it also produces a magnetic effect. The Danish scientist Hans Christian Oersted discovered that whenever an electric current flows through a wire, it produces a magnetic field around the wire. This was shown by a simple experiment: when a current-carrying wire is held over a magnetic compass, the compass needle is deflected (turns aside). When the current is switched off, the needle returns to its normal position. This proves that an electric current behaves like a magnet — this is the magnetic effect of electric current.

The magnetic field around a single straight wire is weak. However, if the wire is wound into a coil of many turns (called a solenoid), the magnetic fields of all the turns add up, producing a much stronger and more useful magnetic field, similar to that of a bar magnet. The strength can be increased even further by placing a piece of soft iron inside the coil.

A coil of insulated wire wound around a soft iron core, which behaves as a magnet only when current flows through it, is called an electromagnet. The great advantage of an electromagnet is that it is a temporary magnet: it acts as a strong magnet when the current is on and loses almost all its magnetism the instant the current is switched off. This makes it possible to switch the magnetism on and off and to control its strength.

The strength of an electromagnet can be increased in three ways: by increasing the number of turns in the coil, by increasing the current flowing through it, and by using a soft iron core inside the coil. Electromagnets have many applications: they are used in electric bells, cranes that lift heavy iron and steel scrap, loudspeakers, electric motors, telephones, and maglev trains, and in devices that separate magnetic metals from waste. The ability to control their magnetism makes them far more useful than ordinary permanent magnets for many machines.

examples.problem: Example 1: A compass needle placed below a wire deflects when current flows and returns to rest when the current stops. What does this experiment prove?
examples.solution:
The compass needle responds to magnetism.

  • The needle is deflected only when current flows in the wire.
  • This shows the current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field around it.
  • Answer: The experiment (Oersted's) proves that an electric current produces a magnetic effect — a magnetic field around the wire.
examples.answer: The experiment (Oersted's) proves that an electric current produces a magnetic effect — a magnetic field around the wire.

examples.problem: Example 2: Why is an electromagnet preferred over a permanent magnet in a crane used to lift iron scrap?
examples.solution:
A scrap-lifting crane must pick up and release loads.

  • An electromagnet is magnetic only while current flows, so it can be switched on to lift the scrap and off to drop it.
  • A permanent magnet is always magnetic and could not release the load easily.
  • Answer: An electromagnet can be switched on and off, so it can pick up the iron scrap and release it on command, unlike a permanent magnet.
examples.answer: An electromagnet can be switched on and off, so it can pick up the iron scrap and release it on command, unlike a permanent magnet.

examples.problem: Example 3: State two ways to increase the strength of an electromagnet.
examples.solution:
The strength depends on the coil and current.

  • Increasing the number of turns in the coil makes it stronger.
  • Increasing the current flowing through the coil also makes it stronger (using a soft iron core helps too).
  • Answer: Increase the number of turns in the coil and increase the current through it (and use a soft iron core).
examples.answer: Increase the number of turns in the coil and increase the current through it (and use a soft iron core).

recap:
• An electric current produces a magnetic field around the conductor — the magnetic effect of current (discovered by Oersted).
  • A coil of many turns (solenoid) produces a much stronger magnetic field than a single straight wire.
  • An electromagnet is a coil wound on a soft iron core that acts as a magnet only while current flows.
  • An electromagnet is a temporary magnet whose magnetism can be switched on and off and controlled.
  • Its strength is increased by more turns, more current, and a soft iron core; uses include bells, cranes, loudspeakers, and motors.

topics.title: The Electric Bell
topics.concept:
The electric bell is a familiar device that puts the magnetic effect of electric current to practical use. It works on the principle of the electromagnet, cleverly arranged so that it rings continuously as long as the switch is pressed. Understanding how it works ties together the ideas of circuits, the magnetic effect, and the electromagnet from this chapter.

The main parts of an electric bell are: an electromagnet (a coil wound on a soft iron core), an armature (a soft iron strip), a hammer attached to the armature, a gong (the metal cup that produces the sound when struck), a contact screw, and a spring that holds the armature. All these are connected in a circuit with a cell and a switch (the push button).

The working can be followed step by step. When the switch is pressed, the circuit is completed and current flows through the coil, turning it into an electromagnet. The electromagnet attracts the soft iron armature, which swings towards it. As the armature moves, the attached hammer strikes the gong, producing a "ring". But the very same movement of the armature breaks the contact at the contact screw, which opens the circuit. With the circuit broken, the current stops, and the electromagnet loses its magnetism. The spring then pulls the armature back to its original position, which remakes the contact and completes the circuit again.

As soon as the contact is remade, current flows once more, the electromagnet attracts the armature again, the hammer strikes the gong again, and the whole cycle repeats — over and over, very rapidly. This make-and-break cycle continues for as long as the switch is kept pressed, so the bell rings continuously. The moment the switch is released, the circuit stays open, the electromagnet has no current, and the bell falls silent. This neat repeating mechanism is why the electric bell is a classic example of the magnetic effect of current in action.

examples.problem: Example 1: On which principle does an electric bell work?
examples.solution:
Consider what makes the hammer move.

  • The hammer is moved by a coil that becomes magnetic when current flows.
  • This coil on a soft iron core is an electromagnet.
  • Answer: An electric bell works on the principle of the electromagnet (the magnetic effect of electric current).
examples.answer: An electric bell works on the principle of the electromagnet (the magnetic effect of electric current).

examples.problem: Example 2: Why does the hammer strike the gong repeatedly rather than just once when the switch is held down?
examples.solution:
The bell uses a make-and-break circuit.

  • When the armature moves to strike the gong, it breaks the contact, switching off the electromagnet, and the spring pulls it back, which remakes the contact.
  • This turns the current on and off rapidly, so the hammer strikes again and again.
  • Answer: The repeated making and breaking of the circuit switches the electromagnet on and off, so the hammer strikes the gong over and over.
examples.answer: The repeated making and breaking of the circuit switches the electromagnet on and off, so the hammer strikes the gong over and over.

examples.problem: Example 3: What happens to the electric bell the moment the push button (switch) is released?
examples.solution:
Releasing the switch affects the circuit.

  • Releasing the switch keeps the circuit open, so no current flows through the coil.
  • With no current, the coil is not an electromagnet and cannot attract the armature.
  • Answer: When the switch is released, the circuit stays open, the electromagnet stops working, and the bell becomes silent.
examples.answer: When the switch is released, the circuit stays open, the electromagnet stops working, and the bell becomes silent.

recap:
• An electric bell works on the principle of the electromagnet (the magnetic effect of electric current).
  • Its main parts are the electromagnet, armature, hammer, gong, contact screw, and spring, in a circuit with a cell and switch.
  • Pressing the switch sends current through the coil, making it an electromagnet that attracts the armature, so the hammer strikes the gong.
  • The armature's movement breaks the contact, switching off the electromagnet; the spring then pulls it back and remakes the contact.
  • This rapid make-and-break cycle repeats while the switch is pressed, ringing the bell continuously until the switch is released.
